# 230CPS Lockouts — Pleading facts (working)

**Not a pleading. Not legal advice. Not for filing.** Use after **Part 19 leave**. Do **not** caption DG in **153243/2026**.

**These are 2F claims.** 230CPS = the co-op building. **2F** is a three-bedroom apartment. **Bedroom A/B/C** are DG’s floor-plan labels, not building unit IDs. The exclusive room is the one labeled **C**.

**Chronology: complete enough to plead.** Remaining holes (powers order, who emptied C, stock book, 16 May AC reply, 3 Jun door log) are Part 19 / discovery.

---

## Defendants and live counts

| # | Defendant | Claim | Core statute / theory |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C1** | **230 Park South Apartments, Inc.** (Co-op) | Unlawful eviction | **RPAPL 768 + NYC Admin. Code § 26-521** as **one count** — (1)(a) any-person lockout |
| **C2** | Co-op | Treble damages | **RPAPL 853** (separate from C1) |
| **C3** | Co-op | Common-law ouster | Wrongful eviction + trespass to **possession of Bedroom C** |
| **E1** | **IR’s estate**, AC **as property guardian** | Owner restore | **RPAPL 768(1)(b) / 26-521** restore |
| **E2** | Estate (AC as guardian) | **Oral sublease of Bedroom C** / QE | IR→DG demise of C; **not** board-approved. Art. 15 gap is **IR’s**. Guest chaos; **actual** eviction 3 Jun |
| **E3** | Estate (AC as guardian) | Quantum meruit | Caregiving / safety beyond the room bargain |
| **E4** | Estate (AC as guardian) | Promissory estoppel | **685 First Ave**; IR’s **$5k/month**. **4F is not a second PE count** |
| **E5** | Estate (AC as guardian) | Negligent failure to control invitees | Force-entry / midnight “evict” / guest-period theft-damage. **In the alternative, after leave.** Not habitability. Not G2 |
| **G1** | **AC individually** | Unlawful eviction / assist | **768(1)(a)** any person who evicts **or assists**; (iii) removing possessions **if emptying proved** |
| **G2** | AC individually | Chattel | Conversion **or alt.** replevin **or alt.** bailment |

**Leave:** Part 19 sealed OSC before suing AC individually **and** as guardian, and before suing IR/estate. Co-op is the 3 Jun **door** actor. **Owner** for 768(1)(b) = **shareholder (IR / estate)**; AC answers as guardian. Co-op is **not** the primary 768(1)(b) owner.

**Do not caption:** MK, RL, NK, JB, individual directors, Nasca, Blake. **Do not plead:** attornment; TPG inherits IR’s shoes; criminal-report forbearance as room consideration; 2F sold; restore-occupancy prayer; MK emptying on hearsay.

---

## Do not put in a verified complaint

- Penal Law § 215.45 (criminal-report forbearance as Bedroom C rent). 16 Jan 2026 letter’s law-enforcement sentence **will be produced**; demand letter, not the theory.
- Board-approved Art. 15 sublease (oral IR→DG demise of **C** **is** pleaded as to the estate; consent failure is **IR’s**). DG = Nasca; DG = 16 May “two people.”
- Separate promissory-estoppel count on **4F** (no signed deal, no keys; DG rejected the 3 Oct re-trade). 4F is sequence / $6k corroboration. E4 = **685**.
- IIED, fraud, interference, constructive eviction / public nuisance / **RPL 235-b habitability** as standalone, board fiduciary to occupant, stacked fines, emergency lien.
- Guest force-entry, midnight “evict,” or theft **lumped only into QE/habitability**. Split: E2 = disturbance in possession; **E5** = duty to control invitees; actor-level intent if captioned; **G2** = emptying after 3 Jun only.

# 685 First Avenue relocation — promissory-estoppel facts (revised working draft)

**Not a pleading. Not legal advice. Not for filing without counsel review and exhibit checking.**  
**Scope:** This is the factual sequence for the proposed **E4 relocation/promissory-estoppel** claim against IR’s estate, after Part 19 leave. It concerns **685 First Avenue**. It does not create a separate claim concerning 4F or 18C.

## Proposed factual allegations

1. In early 2024, Ian Reisner engaged Daniel George to lead work connected with the opening and operation of the hotel at 510 West 42nd Street.

2. The parties’ working arrangement included a monthly cash retainer, a housing benefit, and discussions of future equity. On March 4, 2024, Reisner placed the value of a room such as the hotel room occupied by George at approximately **$5,000 per month**.

3. George occupied hotel room #209 while performing the hotel work. On September 6, 2024, people acting in connection with the hotel excluded George from that room.

4. On September 6, 2024, Reisner invited George to stay at Apartment 2F, 230 Central Park South. Reisner wrote: “Take a nap at my house”; “2F is in mint condition”; and asked whether George needed “a place to stay at 230 Central Park south for tonight.” George arrived at 230 Central Park South that afternoon and occupied the room later identified as **2F Bedroom C**.

5. George’s occupancy of Bedroom C provided interim housing while Reisner and George addressed replacement housing. The parties’ arrangement for Bedroom C consisted of civil forbearance concerning claims arising from the 510 West 42nd Street events and services George had rendered in connection with the hotel enterprise.

6. On September 10, 2024, Reisner discussed Apartment 18C as a possible housing alternative. The 18C discussion formed the first step in the parties’ relocation sequence.

7. The parties next discussed Apartment 4F as a possible temporary location. On September 18, 2024, Reisner described the 4F transaction as an acquisition still in progress. On September 25, 2024, Reisner wrote McKenzie Ryan to ask for a few minutes of access to 4F and for an update concerning keys.

8. On September 26, 2024, Reisner discussed a one-bedroom apartment at approximately $5,000 per month near Central Park South. George identified **685 First Avenue**, specifically an east-facing R-line apartment, as the replacement residence he sought.

9. Reisner agreed to participate in the 685 First Avenue application as George’s guarantor. On the evening of September 26, 2024, On-Site sent Reisner an email inviting him to participate in the application as co-applicant/guarantor. Reisner forwarded that message to George.

10. On September 27, 2024, at approximately 1:30 p.m., George’s application for 685 First Avenue was submitted. George applied for the apartment, and Reisner was identified as the guarantor. George paid the application-related fees.

11. The 685 materials in the file identify east-facing R/S-line apartments with gross monthly pricing in the approximate range of **$4,900 to $5,050**. That pricing corresponds to the $5,000 monthly replacement-housing figure Reisner discussed on September 26.

12. The guarantor application required financial materials from Reisner. The 685 application remained incomplete at the guarantor stage, and the building did not issue George a lease.

13. On October 3, 2024, Reisner addressed the 685 housing arrangement and his ability to provide “United Nations” housing. During the same exchange, Reisner again raised a short-term 4F arrangement. George responded, “I’m not renegotiating this again.”

14. George continued to occupy Bedroom C while the 685 First Avenue application remained unresolved.

15. During that interim occupancy, Reisner’s guests and associates repeatedly disrupted George’s use of 2F and created material safety concerns.

16. On October 31, 2024, an associate of Reisner stated that there was “lots of money in there”

**IR’s bid was $4MM.** He posted **$1.5MM earnest in late February 2024** and became **purchaser / assignee-designate**. He did **not** then have the remaining **$2.5MM**. # CPLR 215(3) and 204(a) — working note (not advice)

**Not a pleading. Not a conclusion.** Counsel must brief. Controlling memos stay in charge. This note answers: *how would 215(3) even apply*, and *what 204(a) actually does to the clock*.

**Do not** ask Part 19 to rewrite 215 against **ML / JB / MK / RL**. **Do** ask Part 19 to **declare or grant** a 204(a) exclusion vs **estate / UR** for **23 Apr 2025 – 17 Apr 2026** (unknowns **P6**). Unsigned Aug 2025 toll draft is **not** a toll.

---

## 1. What CPLR 215(3) actually says

CPLR **215** is the **one-year** basket. Subdivision **(3)** is a **closed list**:

> an action to recover damages for **assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, libel, slander, false words causing special damages, or a violation of the right of privacy** under Civil Rights Law § 51.

**It does not name** unlawful eviction, RPAPL **768**, RPAPL **853**, conversion, replevin, quiet enjoyment, contract, promissory estoppel, quantum meruit, housing harassment, or negligent supervision.

So 215(3) **does not “apply” to the 2F case as a whole.** It applies only if a **count is one of those listed torts**, or if a court **analogizes** a damages statute to that list.

### What *would* be a true 215(3) count in this file

| Count / fact | 215(3)? | Clock (no toll) | File |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RL copier shove 17 Jun 2024** (assault/battery) | **Yes** | ~**17 Jun 2025** | **510 only.** Parked as a 230 count |
| ML “bash your head in” (**30 Jun–2 Jul 2024**) | **Yes as a separate 215(3) assault count** (imminent apprehension). **Also** 768(1)(a)(i) + H4. Dual-plead — §7 | ~**30 Jun / 2 Jul 2025** vs **ML personally** (no 204) | **510 only.** Do not recast as ML’s negligence |
| Brad Reisner knife **11/28/2024** if captioned as assault | **Yes, if so pleaded** | ~**28 Nov 2025** | **Not** a live 2F count. E2/E5 color |
| **False imprisonment** | Only if DG was **confined in** a place | n/a | A **lockout is exclusion from** the unit, not confinement **in** it. Poor fit |
| Libel / slander / CRL 51 | Not pleaded | — | — |

**Do not recast** the shove or “bash your head in” as the **actors’** negligence to dodge 215. Those stay intentional as to the people who did them (510 memo §4A).

**CPLR 215(8)** (extra year after a **criminal** case against the **same defendant** for the **same event**) is **not** a working salvage: *People v. Lupo* CR-700575-25CN complainant was **IR**, not DG. No criminal companion on the copier or the lockouts is in the file.

**CPLR 215(4)** is a **different** one-year box: a **statutory penalty or forfeiture given wholly or partly to any person who will prosecute** (informer-style). A defendant *may* try to stuff **768(2) civil penalties** ($1,000–$10,000; $100/day restore, cap six months) into 215(4). That is **not** 215(3). Plaintiff’s better home is **CPLR 214(2)** (three years — liability/penalty created by statute **except** as provided in 213 and 215). **Counsel briefs the 214(2) vs 215(4) fight.** Do not concede 215(4).

---

## 2. Why the file kept saying “215” next to 768 / 853

Because New York **case law**, not the text of 215(3), treats **RPAPL 853 treble-damages** as a **one-year intentional-tort** claim:

- *Kolomensky v. Wiener*, 135 A.D.2d 505 (2d Dep’t 1987) — 853 is **not** CPLR 213(1) or 214(2); one year because it seeks recovery for an **intentional tort**.
- *Gold v. Schuster*, 264 A.D.2d 547 (1st Dep’t 1999) — “wrongful eviction” damages claims governed by the **one-year** period applicable to intentional torts; accrues when it is reasonably certain the occupant has been **unequivocally removed** with at least implicit denial of a right to return.
- *PK Rest., LLC v. Lifshutz*, 138 A.D.3d 434 (1st Dep’t 2016); *Parker v. Howard Ave. Realty, LLC*, 55 Misc. 3d 101 (App. Term 2d Dep’t 2017) — same one-year for **853-style damages**.

Those opinions often say “one-year / intentional tort” **without quoting 215(3)**. Secondary sources then **mislab

# Claim-exclusion and relief audit — 23 August 2026

**Purpose.** This audit tests the reasons the working file has *not* pleaded certain theories. It is a litigation-screening document, not legal advice or a filing instruction. “Exclude” means “do not plead on the present record,” not “the event did not happen.” A claim should be reconsidered only if new evidence supplies a distinct defendant, duty, injury, and remedy.

## Executive conclusion

Most of the exclusions are sound and strategically valuable. They prevent the focused 2F occupant/lockout/property case from being recast as a sensational, overlapping, or conclusory dispute. A few are better described as **reserved** rather than permanently rejected:

- 230 tenant-harassment, declaratory/injunctive preservation, and targeted pre-action disclosure are possible procedural/remedial tools if needed, but they should not be added merely to create more counts.
- Hotel-enterprise constructive trust/accounting and identity-use theories belong, if at all, in the later **510/estate** case after Part 19 leave—not the 2F pleading.
- The remedy strategy should no longer request present physical restoration to Bedroom C as the default. The Part 19 request can instead seek **leave, information, accounting, preservation, and property production**, while preserving the legal consequences of the failure to restore.

---

### A. “Attornment” to the co-op

**Working exclusion: sound.**

Attornment would assert a new direct tenancy between DG and the co-op after IR’s proprietary-lease status changed. The present facts instead support: (1) IR’s permission for Bedroom C; (2) DG’s asserted 30-day occupant rights; and (3) the co-op’s notice/knowledge of occupancy. Those are materially different propositions.

**Why it should stay out:**

- No agreement, rent arrangement, or acceptance by the co-op supports a new direct tenancy.
- It would invite the co-op to litigate the end of IR’s proprietary lease and to characterize DG as seeking benefits of a tenancy he says was never made.
- It is unnecessary to statutory occupant protection: a lawful occupant need not prove a new co-op tenancy to challenge a warrantless exclusion.

**What remains usable:** co-op knowledge—doormen’s-logbook permission, staff familiarity, and the June 3 instruction—supports the lockout theory and defeats a claim that DG was an unknown overnight visitor.

---

### B. Board-approved 2024 2F sublet

**Working exclusion: sound and important.**

The 2019 4F board package establishes only that DG had a prior legitimate connection to the building. It cannot be converted into consent to DG’s 2024 occupancy of 2F. The record does not contain a 2024 Art. 15 package, board vote, proprietary-lease consent, or signed sublease.

**Proper narrower theory:** oral IR-to-DG demise of **Bedroom C**, or alternatively exclusive licensee/roommate status. Any failure by IR to seek co-op consent is IR’s issue vis-à-vis the co-op; it does not itself authorize self-help against a 270-day occupant.

---

### C. Criminal-report forbearance as consideration

**Working exclusion: essential.**

The 16 January 2026 demand-letter wording about forgoing law-enforcement reporting must not become the consideration alleged for the room. Such a pleading would create an avoidable illegality/public-policy problem and make the central occupancy theory look coercive.

Respondent **acknowledges and admits** that:

- **(a)** Respondent is in possession of the **entire building** 510 W 42 (the “Premises”);

- **(c)** Respondent is **not aware of any other persons and/or entities having any rights to or claims against the Premises**.

¶3 withdraws fictitious undertenants ABC/XYZ **without prejudice**. ¶10 (going forward): no occupancy except UR, hotel guests in the ordinary course, and permitted subtenants.

**Working answer: yes — as to DG, it is false or at least knowingly incomplete.** It is **UR’s** representation (Kaiser signed). It is **not** a finding that DG had no 768 rights. Do **not** plead a fraud count against Kaiser/UR off this paper unless asked.

# Claude for Legal — workflow adoption note

**Reviewed repository:** `anthropics/claude-for-legal`, main branch as accessed 23 August 2026.  
**Purpose:** Evaluate workflow ideas for this DG case file. This is not an installation, legal advice, or authority to connect any third-party service to confidential case data.

## Bottom line

The most useful part of the repository is **not a legal-rule engine or case-management system**. It is a set of prompt/workflow templates that enforce good litigation-file discipline: separate matters, append-only event history, source-pinned chronologies, element-by-element claim charts, conservative gap flags, preservation tracking, and explicit review gates before consequential acts.

That discipline matches the needs of this case file. The repository should be used as an **architecture reference**, not copied wholesale or connected to the case material without a confidentiality/security review.

## High-value workflow ideas for this file

| Repository capability | DG adaptation | Immediate value |
|---|---|---|
| **Matter workspace / matter briefing** | Maintain separate matter records for **230 CPS**, **510 W 42**, and a shared **Part 19 / preservation** workstream. Cross-reference them; do not merge claims. | Prevents the existing two-dwelling record from collapsing into one narrative. |
| **Chronology with significance and source tags** | Rebuild the current prose chronologies into a source ledger with: Date; event; source file/page/message; source type; person with personal knowledge; fact status; relevance; privilege/confidentiality flag; open verification. | Converts the strong narrative file into a pleading and discovery tool. |
| **Civil claim chart** | One chart per prospective count. Each row: element; controlling NY authority/statute; fact; primary exhibit/pinpoint; authentication witness; defense; gap; limitations; requested relief. | Tests pleading sufficiency and avoids duplicative or stale claims. |
| **Matter briefing** | Generate a dated one-page briefing before counsel meetings: procedural posture, last change, next deadline, urgent evidence, decisions needed, and risk re-assessment. | Replaces reopening many long memos to answer routine status questions. |
| **Legal-hold workflow** | Draft—but do not send without counsel—a personal preservation checklist for DG and, where appropriate, a counsel-reviewed preservation demand for outside custodians. | Preserves raw texts, email metadata, original PDFs, photographs, PNR/booking records, and device/cloud exports. |
| **Docket watcher** | Maintain a manual docket-watch log for Part 19, Nasca, LT-316530, and the specific related 510 matters. | Captures the next known event: *Nasca* hearing, 27 October 2026, while avoiding intervention. |
| **Demand-letter / brief drafting gates** | Preserve a required review gate: no filing, service, demand, public narrative, or insurance tender from a draft without attorney review and source verification. | Particularly important here because some records are sealed, privileged, sensitive, or based on DG’s recollection. |

## Proposed local structure — do not install anything yet

A small, case-specific structure in this repository is preferable to adopting the plugin’s in-house corporate portfolio model literally:

# Affirmation of Daniel S. George

SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK  
COUNTY OF NEW YORK — IAS Part 19

In the Matter of the Application for the Appointment of a Guardian  
for IAN S. REISNER, an Incapacitated Person.

**SEALED**

DANIEL S. GEORGE, non-party applicant.

---

STATE OF NEW YORK  
COUNTY OF NEW YORK

DANIEL S. GEORGE, affirms the following to be true under the penalties of perjury, pursuant to CPLR 2106:

**1.** I am Daniel S. George. I make this affirmation in support of my application for leave to sue, and for the related relief in the proposed order. I have personal knowledge of the facts stated here except where I say otherwise.

**2.** This application concerns two places I occupied, and property I left in each: a hotel room, **510 West 42nd Street #209**, and a bedroom in **Apartment 2F, 230 Central Park South**, which I call **2F Bedroom C**. The claims I ask leave to bring are listed in Exhibit A. They run against Ian S. Reisner’s estate, Urban Resort LLC, and Andre K. Cizmarik, Esq., as property guardian and individually.

---

### The hotel and room 209

**3.** In or about March 2024, Ian Reisner asked me to serve as project lead to convert and open a hotel at 510 West 42nd Street. The operating company was Urban Resort LLC, also known as Cachet and as the Hudson Yards Hotel. I did that work as an independent contractor. I was not an employee.

**4.** The arrangement was a $10,000 monthly retainer, a $5,000 monthly housing benefit, and a discussion of equity. Ian paid the retainer for March through June 2024 only — $40,000, by wires from IR Holdings and then Urban Resort. The housing benefit was never paid in cash. After June 2024 I was not paid the retainer either.

**5.** From mid-March 2024 I lived in room 209 at the hotel while I did that work. I paid no cash rent. What I gave for the room was my services, expertise, and labor on the project.

**6.** On July 10, 2024, my key to #209 stopped working. Jeremy Broderick directed desk staff not to cut a new key. I called the police. The CAD numbers are 104511787, 104511949, and 104512967. Glenn Isaacs, who represents the landowner, told the officers that day that I had every right to be there and that my occupancy predated Urban Resort’s lease. The police restored access on July 11. By then belongings had already been taken from the room.

**7.** On September 6, 2024, I was locked out of #209 again. Broderick was involved. Michal Kravarik was in the lobby. That lockout has never been undone. I have not been restored to #209.

---

### 2F Bedroom C

**8.** The same afternoon, September 6, 2024, Ian texted me to come to his apartment, 2F at 230 Central Park South. He asked if I needed a place to stay. I went there. That night I occupied the south-end bedroom — about 8 feet 7 inches by 13 feet, with its own bath. On my floor plan that room is Bedroom C. I occupied it exclusively from that night until I was barred from the building on June 3, 2025 — 270 days.

**9.** I paid no cash rent for 2F Bedroom C. What I gave Ian in return was forbearance of civil claims arising from the 510 lockouts, from conversion of my property, and from other wrongs connected with the hotel, together with services I had already rendered and continued to render.

**10.** The building knew I lived there. On September 19, 2024, Ian said he would tell the doorman to let me up. Permission was written in the doormen’s logbook. Staff already knew me from earlier dealings at 230 Central Park South.

**11.** For much of those 270 days I lived in 2F with Ian. He used the master bedroom. I used Bedroom C. After he left the apartment in February 2025, I remained in Bedroom C with his permission. We had discussed term; he said nothing was allowed for less than 30 days. I was there far longer than 30 days.

*

This is not a request that the Court decide the merits, value the claims, restore possession, revive time-barred claims against non-parties, or impose a lien or audit. It is a threshold application, brought in the forum that imposed the stay, by a person who was not noticed and who first learned of the stay two days after he was locked out. The requested relief is cabined to leave, accounting, preservation, and information.

3. After the prior leaseholder became insolvent, the land lease was marketed to the public at $10MM and attracted no offers.

# Matter brief — 230 CPS / Apartment 2F, Bedroom C

**Brief date:** 2026-08-24
**Status:** Pre-suit. No DG action filed. Part 19 leave first as to estate/guardian/UR.
**Controlling memo:** `../../DG_230CPS_Case_File_Memo.md`

> Not a pleading. Not legal advice. Counsel verifies every element, deadline, and pinpoint.

## One-paragraph matter

DG claims exclusive occupancy of one specifically demised room inside Apartment 2F at 230 Central Park South — outwardly "2F Bedroom C" — from 6 September 2024 through 3 June 2025 (270 days) under an oral IR-to-DG demise supported by services and forbearance of civil claims (no cash rent; no board-approved Art. 15 sublet; no attornment). On 3 June 2025, building staff refused DG re-entry, allegedly on co-op counsel Schneider's instruction, with no warrant naming DG. The October 2025 written restore/inventory demand produced AC's written refusal to acknowledge occupancy or allow access, and a statement that property would be inventoried without DG present. The guardian-directed emptying of 2F is supported by Domb's Nasca filing; who handled the property and where it is now remain open.

## Procedural posture

**Purpose:** Local working layer for source control, claim-element mapping, deadlines, and Part 19 relief planning. It supplements the substantive working memos; it does not replace them.

4. **Conflicts remain visible.** Do not overwrite one account with another; add a row and a verification task.

6. **Do not upload sealed, medical, privileged, or discovery-restricted material to a connector without confirming authorization and the applicable order.**

## Source-status legend

| Status | Meaning | Filing use |

| `PRIMARY` | Original email/text/image, docket filing/order, application, original record, or original inventory export | Pinpoint and authenticate |

# Part 19 exhibit-set assembly

**Working-draft assembly tool. Not a filing. Not legal advice. Counsel to conform, authenticate, seal, and replace placeholders before any use.**

This folder contains a reproducible build of a sealed exhibit set for the planned
Order to Show Cause in *Matter of Reisner* (Index 500021/2025). It reads the
register at `../exhibit_register.csv`, copies/converts each listed source, stamps
a `GEORGE-PT19-Ex-###` label, and emits one contiguous PDF plus per-exhibit PDFs,
a manifest, a human-readable index, and a list of items still missing.

## Layout

```
assembly/
  assemble_part19.py        # build script (Python 3.11; uses .venv)
  requirements.txt          # pinned deps: pypdf, reportlab, Pillow, xhtml2pdf, Markdown
  README.md                 # this file
  .gitignore                # keeps generated output out of git
  build/                    # generated — safe to delete and rebuild
    GEORGE-PT19-Exhibit-Set.pdf   # one contiguous sealed-style PDF
    INDEX.txt                     # human-readable exhibit index
    MANIFEST.csv                  # per-exhibit status / pages / sha256 / source
    MISSING.txt                   # placeholders and missing sources
  exhibits/                 # generated — one PDF per attached exhibit (cover + body)
  staging/                  # generated — normalized PDFs, extracted Ex A, render fallbacks
```

## How to run

From the repository root:

```bash
# one-time setup (idempotent)
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r case_management/part19/assembly/requirements.txt

# build
.venv/bin/python case_management/part19/assembly/assemble_part19.py
```

The script cleans `build/`, `exhibits/`, and `staging/` on each run, so deleting
folders by hand is not necessary.

## Rendering pipeline

1. Reads a row from `../exhibit_register.csv`.
2. Resolves the source path (supports `;`-separated alternatives, `uploads/`
   fallbacks, and `...` glob shorthand used in the register).
3. Adds a one-page **exhibit cover** identifying the matter, exhibit number,
   title, date, source, and a "working draft" warning.
4. Converts the source to PDF:
   - `.pdf`  → every page is **normalized to US Letter (612 × 792 pt)**. The
     source page is scaled preserving aspect ratio and centered with a 0.4"
     margin; landscape pages are rotated into portrait so they use the page
     width rather than rendering as a tiny strip.
   - `.png/.jpg/.jpeg` → centered Letter-sized image PDF.
   - `.md/.markdown` → rendered through Python-Markdown with the `tables`,
     `fenced_code`, `sane_lists`, `attr_list`, `footnotes`, and `md_in_html`
     extensions, then HTML→PDF via **xhtml2pdf** with a CSS stylesheet.
     Headings, **bold**, *italic*, ordered/unordered lists, tables (with
     borders, header shading, and page-break control), fenced code blocks,
     blockquotes, and horizontal rules render as real typography.
   - `.txt` → HTML-escaped inside a `<pre>` block so whitespace survives.
   - `.csv` → rendered as a styled, multi-page HTML table.
5. **CSV date filtering.** When a register row's `date` cell carries an ISO
   hint like `2025-07-14/16`, `2025-09-04`, or `2026-04-28 18:17`, the script
   parses that inclusive window and — if the CSV has a `Date` column — keeps
   only rows whose date falls within it. So Ex 8 (Jul 14–16), Ex 9 (Sep 4),
   Ex 10 (Sep 19), Ex 11 (Oct 9–10), Ex 29 (Jan 16), Ex 30 (Jan 19),
   Ex 31 (Apr 28), and Ex 32 (Apr 28 OOO) each render only their slice of the
   DG–AC thread instead of all 22 rows. A trailing time of day is ignored;
   the window is whole-day on both ends.
6. Bates-stamps every page with `GEORGE-PT19-Ex-NN` in the lower-right. Because
   every page is now exactly Letter, the stamp lands at the same coordinates
   on every page regardless of source page size.
7. Verifies programmatically that every page in the merged set is exactly
   612 × 792 pt; the run report lists any non-Letter source PDFs that were
   normalized.
8. Records

# Matter brief — Part 19 / Article 81 leave and preservation

**Brief date:** 2026-08-24
**Forum:** Supreme Court, New York County, IAS Part 19 (Sokoloff, J.)
**Index:** 500021/2025 (Article 81 — sealed)
**Status:** Planned sealed OSC; not filed. Counsel captions, dates, service, and sealing.
**Working packet:** `../../DG_Part19_Working_Packet.md`
**Affirmation draft:** `../../DG_Part19_Affirmation_Working_Draft.md`
**Relief matrix:** `relief_matrix.md`
**Source ledger:** `source_ledger.csv`

> Not a pleading. Not legal advice. Counsel verifies every statutory basis, order, service requirement, and sealing protocol. No external action without counsel.

## One-paragraph matter

DG seeks a single sealed Order to Show Cause in the Article 81 proceeding for Ian S. Reisner, covering both 230 CPS (2F Bedroom C) and 510 W 42 (#209 / hotel work / identity). The packet asks for leave to commence defined plenary claims against IR's estate, Urban Resort LLC, and Andre K. Cizmarik (as property guardian and individually for guardian-act conduct); production of the 31 Mar 2025 powers order and the 81.07 service list/petition date; a written two-location chattel account and production of the hotel boxes before any LT-316530 execution; limited non-medical docket access and notice of future property-related applications; a CPLR 204(a) declaration for the 23 Apr 2025 – 17 Apr 2026 stay window against estate/UR only; and a conference/status report. The packet does **not** seek present restoration to Bedroom C, lien priority, a forensic audit of IR entities, or revival of claims against ML, JB, MK, or RL in their personal capacities.

## Procedural posture

- AC appointed temporary property guardian on or about **31 Mar 2025** (actual order not in working set — must obtain).
- Sokoloff stay order on or about **23 Apr 2025** enjoins commencement of claims against AIP and covered LLCs absent sealed Part 19 relief; filed publicly in *Muller v. Reisner*, LT-307189-25, as Doc 14 on 5 Jun 2025. DG first saw it there.
- DG was a 2F cohabitant at petition/temporary appointment and states he was never served or given MHL §81.07 notice.
- DG's 14 Jul 2025 first email to AC; 4 Sep 2025 draft equitable pleadings; 9/19 Sep tolling discussion (AC said judge wanted more detail; no toll signed); 9–10 Oct 2025 call scheduling and the mid-October call where AC allegedly said he was not paid to investigate, could not resolve claims then, and someone would contact DG when capacity was determined.
- 20–22 Oct 2025 written restore/inventory demand and AC's written refusal/qualified response.
- 19 Jan 2026 AC email about segregated hotel boxes; inspection never occurred.
- Permanent guardian appointed 17 Apr 2026 (actual order needed). DG followed up 28 Apr 2026 — only AC's 24 Apr–5 May OOO reply is in the file.
- No signed tolling agreement. A 29 Aug 2025 draft was never signed/so-ordered.

# Preservation checklist — personal case records

**Draft checklist for counsel review.** This is an organizational aid, not a legal-hold notice and not a direction to alter, export, access, or disclose another person’s systems. Preserve lawfully held originals in their native form where possible. Do not delete, edit, crop, annotate, forward, or overwrite originals.

## DG-controlled material to preserve

| Category | Preserve | Preferred form | Reason / related workstream |
|---|---|---|---|
| Text/iMessage/WhatsApp | Full threads, contact cards, timestamps, attachments, export/backups, device identifiers | Native export + read-only copy + PDF for review | 6 Sep invitation; 685; Oct-Dec 2F events; 10 Jul/6 Sep 510 events; identity objections |
| Email | Original .eml/.msg, headers, attachments, sent and received copies | Native message + PDF; maintain folder path | AC demand/refusal chain; Hunter; 685; deck/identity; payments |
| Photos/video | Original files with metadata; all angles and surrounding context | Original HEIC/JPEG/video + hash/read-only copy | Bedroom C, property, door notices, listings, condition |
| Travel/booking | PNR, confirmation, purchase timestamp, itinerary, card records | Original emails/PDF/account export | Dates relevant to 3 Jun and July 2024 chronology |
| Financial/property records | Payment confirmations, receipts, inventory source CSV/Notion exports, purchase records | Original export/statement; preserve formulas and metadata | Separate 2F and 510 chattel/value proof; retainer/expense proof |
| Docket/website material | Downloaded filing/PDF plus URL, access date, docket number/document number | PDF + capture log | Nasca, Part 19-related public filing, LT-316530, listings |
| Phone/call material | Call logs, voicemails, contemporaneous notes | Original device export; dated note | 3 Jun and October 2025 conversations |

## Preservation protocol

1. Create read-only duplicate copies; retain originals unchanged.
2. Record each collection in a simple log: date collected, collector, source device/account, filename, hash if available, and related ledger ID.
3. Keep original and review copy separate. Do not add highlights/comments to originals.
4. Do not access accounts, devices, premises, cloud folders, or records without authorization.
5. Do not use screenshots as a substitute when a native export is available.
6. Do not put sealed Article 81 materials, medical materials, privileged communications, or discovery-restricted materials into third-party AI, cloud, or connector tools without counsel authorization.
7. Before producing anything externally, have counsel determine authenticity, privilege, confidentiality, protective-order restrictions, and completeness.

## High-priority missing originals

- Original 6 Sep, 19 Sep, 26 Sep–3 Oct 2024 IR/DG relocation messages.
- Original October–December 2024 2F safety/guest messages, including the NS 4 Dec message.
- 3 Jun 2025 contemporaneous call logs, notes, any building/NYPD material lawfully held.
- Full October 20–22, 2025 and January/April 2026 AC email chains including headers/attachments.
- Original 685 application, fee proof, On-Site forward, and pricing materials.
- Source CSV/Notion export behind each separate chattel schedule.
- Original April/October 2024 deck and identity-use emails.

## External preservation requests

Any request to a co-op, guardian, hotel, insurer, broker, service provider, or counsel must be drafted and sent only after counsel decides the legal basis, recipient, scope, privilege implications, and timing. The Part 19 relief matrix identifies the narrowest current information/property targets.

Ian Reisner (IR) and Dan George (DG) frequently discussed the settlement of claims related to DG's compensation and housing, particularly as IR's financial situation and behavior became more erratic. These discussions often revolved around unpaid amounts, unfulfilled promises, and the consequences of actions taken by IR's associates.
Here are key excerpts detailing their discussions on these matters:
Early Discussions and Unfulfilled Promises (March - September 2024):
• Initial Offers and Shortfalls (March 2024): In early March 2024, IR enlisted DG to reopen the 510 W 42nd Street hotel, which was vacant and vandalized. IR had recently acquired a contractual interest in the lease and relied entirely on DG to restore the asset and salvage his interest. DG proposed an interim salary of $250,000/year with a $50,000 upfront draw, half allocated as a contingency due to IR’s unreliability. IR never paid more than ~$45,000 in sporadic tranches, and DG personally advanced many reopening costs. IR consistently acknowledged DG's essential role, stating the reopening would not have happened without him. Despite asking DG to propose his compensation and assuring him he would be an "executive in Urban Resort LLC for the long time" (implying future equity), IR balked at the $250K figure, citing a cash crunch.
• Varying Compensation Proposals: IR's compensation proposals varied wildly, from "$100K plus food stamps" to $1000/day to revenue shares, none of which were fulfilled. Housing was always part of the compensation structure because the work required relocation and Reisner claimed to have very little cash.
• Housing as Promised Compensation: Housing was a promised benefit, initially on-site at the hotel and later at IR’s apartment, but these promises were not reliably honored, and at times were not even within IR’s ability to grant. DG was illegally locked out of his home without notice on three occasions.
• Unresolved Issues and Threats of Legal Action (July - September 2024):
    ◦ In July 2024, DG implored IR to intervene after his associates (Jeremy Broderick, Maureen Lupo, and Richard Lemmerman) interfered with DG's work and caused harm, but IR remained largely absent and passive due to his addiction. DG warned IR that if Jeremy, "Baby" (Maureen Lupo), or anyone else purporting to act on his behalf did not comply with the law, he would involve the NYPD.
    ◦ On September 10, 2024, DG told IR that the exploitation by his associates needed to stop, stating, "You aren’t seeing things clearly. That’s not something that can be resolved in a day". He highlighted that solving IR's problems created problems for him and that his labor was being "shorted".
    ◦ On September 12, 2024, DG reminded IR of "unresolved issues, the two unlawful evictions, false allegations by Jeremy about taking money from rental of room, recap of concerns about preceding events involving Broderick, Lupo and Lemmerman". IR offered DG to move into his apartment (230 CPS 2F), which DG declined due to it not being private or secure. DG emphasized that the situation "must be resolved before DG returns to NYC after one week forbearance period". IR said cash came in from a Fire Island Pines account closure, and he "wants to pay me and pay for accommodations and for my legal retainer for insurance coverage counsel as originally promised in early 2024".
    ◦ On September 18, 2024, DG outlined three discussion points: "1. Funding the insurance recovery work. $30k. 2. Resolving the housing emergency created by GI Joe’s two illegal eviction attempts. (It has now been nearly two weeks unresolved, and I will have to involve NYPD if we don’t come to a relocation agreement.) 3. A general release for you for all claims and work related to the hotel — though we don’t need to resolve this one today". IR responded that he would pay $2500 as "severance", stating that was what he had asked his team to give DG anyway. DG clarified that "$2500 is earnest money, not a settlement in full"

#### Oral Lease Construction

1. In September 2024, IR granted DG explicit permission to enter and reside in a private unit (later reduced to a private room) at 230CPS, following the second of two unlawful evictions conducted by his unscrupulous associates at another property. (See 510W42 Background).  
2. In exchange, DG agreed to temporarily suspend filing of substantive claims against IR, associated entities and persons while the parties negotiated a mutually agreeable and durable settlement.  
3. The interim agreement included an oral sublease immediately enforceable and in place until such time as a permanent settlement could be reached, or negotiations abandoned in favor of a judicial determination.  
4. DG believed IR had the ability to grant the sublease and relied on IR’s representations that he did.  
5. IR believed and represented to DG that a board application for DG’s subtenancy was not required because IR owned unsold shares, exempting him from certain rules governing the co-op following its conversion in 1983\.  
6. Whether IR made material misrepresentations to DG in the construction of the sublease is immaterial to the claims stated herein.  
7. First, IR offered DG 18C, an apartment which was occupied by a rent control tenant and uninhabitable.  
8. Next, IR offered DG apartment 3F, which IR did not own but said he was imminently purchasing.  
9. Subsequently, IR offered DG private Bedroom C in 2F, pending other mutually agreeable relocation arrangements. (See 2F Floor Plan).  
10. At the time, Bedroom A was used by IR, and Bedroom B was sublet to IR’s roommate, RW.  
11. As IR’s propositions became increasingly unfavorable for DG, DG requested to be relocated to a rental building with a reliable landlord.   
12. IR told DG to shop for an apartment of equal value to the unit from which he had been displaced, which had a stated value of $5k per month.  
13. DG identified a suitable rental apartment at 685 First Ave, which IR agreed to rent for DG as part of the parties’ settlement agreement under active negotiation.   
14. IR completed some but not all of the financial paperwork required to lease the apartment at 685 First Ave before he left New York for a few weeks for medical treatment.  
15. While IR was away for medical treatment, DG and RW remained home in 2F, and it was a peaceful and relatively normal 10 days.  
16. When IR returned, he still needed significant supportive cognitive supervision, home health and hygiene maintenance services, and safety protocols – in addition to business guidance.  
17. DG supported such unmet needs to an extraordinary degree beyond the scope of any agreement.  
18. IR never completed the paperwork required to lease the apartment at 685 First Ave and DG remained in 2F under the interim agreement.  
19. The interim agreement remains in effect until a durable settlement, which includes relocation and return of DG’s chattel, has been completed.  
    

#### The Building’s Knowledge of DG’s Residency

20. DG had previously rented 2F in its entirety from IR in 2019\. DG and his pug-beagle mix “Jaws” were well-known to the doormen and building staff.   
21. As a licensed real estate agent and media professional, DG had also previously marketed other units, negotiated leases and submitted board packages for several other 230CPS shareholders and tenants.  
22. From time to time, DG prepared presentations for and/or presented proposals to the 230CPS board in 2018 and 2019\.  
23. When DG returned to 230CPS as a subtenant of 2F, building staff accepted DG’s mail, announced his visitors, and frequently sought his help to “rein in” IR’s objectionable conduct within the building.  
24. DG’s occupancy was recorded in the doormen’s logbook, which contained his phone number so that visitors and packages could be announced.  
25. The building superintendent, other maintenance workers, and various third parties visited apartment 2F while DG was a resident.

#### Increasing Dangers in 2F
